eVideos.videoDescription:
This is the fourth video in my series on Apple’s Foundation Models Framework.
If you haven’t watched the first three videos, I highly recommend doing that first — we’ll be using and expanding on the code built earlier in the series.

In this tutorial, we’ll create a fully interactive travel agent chatbot that uses Apple’s on-device intelligence to respond to your questions. You’ll learn how to:
• Use the LanguageModelSession transcript to manage conversation history
• Display chat-style bubbles for both user and agent messages
• Implement thinking indicators and automatic scroll behavior
• Handle model availability and error responses
• Enforce Guardrails to prevent inappropriate prompts

By the end of this video, you’ll have a working chatbot that feels intelligent, natural, and fun to use — powered entirely by Apple’s Foundation Models Framework.
eVideos.video: Using SwiftUI Foundation Models Transcripts to build a Chatbot

eVideos.videoDescription:
In this third instalment of the Foundations Model series, I’ll show you how to use guided generation to produce structured, type-safe AI responses instead of freeform text.

We’ll build two examples:
1. A FitnessPal-style workout generator that produces an array of exercises using enums, sliders, and guided macros.
2. A Topic Title Generator that streams results live and gracefully handles errors when safety guardrails are triggered.

You’ll learn how to:
 • Use the @Generable and @Guide macros
 • Combine global instructions with user prompts
 • Stream partial results with Foundation Models
 • Handle model availability and guardrail errors
 • Build structured, predictable AI-driven views in SwiftUI

If you haven’t watched the first two videos in the series, I recommend starting there — links are in the description.
Download the starter and completed projects from GitHub and follow along!
eVideos.video: Guided Generation with Foundation Models in Swift — Structured AI Responses

eVideos.videoDescription:
This is the second video in my series on Apple’s Foundation Models Framework.
If you haven’t watched the first one yet, I highly recommend starting there—you’ll need some of the setup and code we created.

In this follow-up, we’ll build an interactive Prompt Builder that lets you select prompt criteria like workout type and duration using a picker and slider, while providing real-time feedback with disabled buttons, progress indicators, and markdown handling in SwiftUI.

You’ll also learn how to:
• Use the PromptBuilder API for structured prompts
• Manage UI state while waiting for model responses
• Stream AI responses as they’re generated with smooth animation
• Clean up markdown output for SwiftUI text rendering
• Preload and warm up sessions for faster responses
eVideos.video: Foundation Models Framework Part 2  Prompt Builders, Streaming & UI Feedback

eVideos.videoDescription:
Apple introduced the Foundation Models Framework at WWDC25, giving developers direct access to Apple’s on-device large language model with native Swift support. In this video, I’ll show you how to get started by embedding the model into your app in just a few lines of code.
We’ll cover:
• Setting up the project with a starter branch
• Using LanguageModelSession to send prompts and receive responses
• Handling errors and Apple’s built-in safety guardrails
• Checking device and OS requirements for Apple Intelligence
• Building a reusable service for availability checks

This is the first part of a multi-video series exploring the power of Foundation Models for Swift developers.
eVideos.video: Foundation Models Framework in Swift  Getting Started with On Device AI

eVideos.videoDescription: Beginning Oct 16, I will begin releasing a 5 part series on using Foundation Model for SwiftUI.  You will learn the fundamentals of using  theFoundation Model framework to use Apples on device machine learning models in your SwiftUI apps.

Apple has expanded SwiftUI’s shape capabilities in iOS 26 and macOS 15 with the new ConcentricRectangle API and its companion clip shape for concentric corners.
These new tools give developers more creative control than ever before—letting you move beyond sharp edges and uniform radii to adaptive corner curves that respond to their container.

In this video, I’ll walk you through:
• Creating and customizing concentric rectangles with different initializers
• Using concentric corners in clip shapes to transform any view
• Controlling corners individually with minimum radii
• Embedding shapes in container shapes like rounded rectangles and capsules
• Applying concentric corners in sheets, popovers, and modal presentations
• A bonus: splitting an image into a tiled grid with rounded corners
eVideos.video: SwiftUI Concentric Rectangle & Concentric Corners in iOS 26

eVideos.videoDescription:
In my previous video, we built a simple SwiftUI WebView using just a URL, but that approach has its limits. In this follow-up, we unlock the full potential of WebPage in SwiftUI’s new WebKit integration.

You’ll learn how to:
• Display page titles dynamically as you navigate
• Show a loading progress bar with smooth transitions
• Load custom HTML directly from strings or from files in your bundle
• Use a URLRequest for full control over headers, caching, and HTTP methods
• Add back and forward navigation buttons, plus reload and stop controls
• Implement history tracking with context menus for quick jumps
• Restrict navigation to a specific host domain with a custom navigation decider

We’ll build everything step-by-step, starting from a simple tab layout and ending with a feature-rich, customizable browser component.
eVideos.video: SwiftUI WebPage — Advanced Navigation, Loading, and HTML Control

eVideos.videoDescription:
In this tutorial, we explore the new SwiftUI WebKit and its powerful WebView with a URL argument. You’ll learn how to:
• Build a simple but feature-rich web browser in SwiftUI
• Validate and auto-correct URLs before loading
• Configure keyboard behavior for URL entry
• Show a “content unavailable” view for unreachable sites
• Add a scroll-to-top button that appears dynamically
• Enable or disable navigation gestures, magnification, previews, and text selection through a configuration sheet

We’ll start with a basic WebView and progressively add functionality until we have a polished, customizable browsing experience.
Download the starter project from the link in the description and follow along, or grab the completed source code if you prefer to explore at your own pace.
eVideos.video: SwiftUI WebView  (URL Argument) – Features, Validation & More

eVideos.videoDescription:
Apple introduced several subtle yet powerful updates to TabView in iOS and iPadOS 26, and in this video, I’ll walk you through them with a hands-on project. You’ll learn how to:
• Design tab-based apps that adapt beautifully across iPhone and iPad
• Use the new liquid glass effect in tab bars
• Create collapsible search tabs and control when the search UI appears
• Add tab bar accessory views and understand when and how they behave
• Adapt layouts for resizable iPad windows using TabViewStyle
• Implement tab bar behavior changes with scroll and keyboard awareness
• Safely add new people to a list with validation and focus management
eVideos.video: TabView in iOS & iPadOS 26: New Features, Search Tabs, and Accessory Views
Mastering iOS 26 Toolbars & Modal Sheets in SwiftUI
eVideos.videoDescription:
iOS 26 brings a fresh take on SwiftUI toolbars and modal presentations, and in this tutorial, I’ll guide you through everything you need to know. We’ll explore semantic and positional toolbar item placements, new glass button styles, toolbar spacers, and subtitle options—including some quirks to be aware of. You’ll also learn how to use the new matchGeometry transition with modal sheets for a polished, modern experience.

By the end of the video, you’ll be equipped to take full advantage of toolbars and sheet presentation enhancements in iOS 26.

A new web app that lets you explore the contents of my YouTube channel directly in your browser. 
This web app is similar to my dedicated macOS application available on [Gumroad](https://stewartlynch.gumroad.com/l/obsjz), but runs entirely in the browser. 
While it’s not quite as feature-rich as the Mac app, I’ll continue to keep the content updated in both places.  
Features
- 🔎 Search by **title** or **description**
- 🏷️ Filter videos by **tag**
- ▶️ Watch tutorials via embedded YouTube player
- 📂 Access **starter projects** and **source code** links provided with my tutorials  

Instructions for installing on iPhone or iPad:
https://stewartlynch.github.io/YouTube/

Direct link to the web app: https://stewartlynch.github.io/StewartLynchChannel/

eVideos.video: Mastering SwiftUI’s New Glassy Controls in iOS 26 – Toggles, Sliders & Menus
eVideos.videoDescription:
In the latest instalment of my OS 26 liquid glass design series, we go beyond buttons and dive into polished control updates across SwiftUI:
• Toggles with floating glass bubbles
• Segmented pickers that react to drag gestures
• Sliders with tick marks, both fixed and dynamically generated
• Menus & Submenus, redesigned with leading‑edge icons and frosted‑glass overlays
• A plus‑to‑check transition add‑button for lists using SwiftUI geometry matching

eVideos.video: Mastering Liquid Glass in SwiftUI – Buttons, Containers & Transitions
eVideos.videoDescription:
SwiftUI’s Liquid Glass effect in OS 26 is more than just eye candy—it’s a whole new design system. In this tutorial, I’ll guide you through the new button styles, applying glass effects to various views, and using GlassEffectContainer to create seamless, fluid layouts.

We’ll also explore namespace-powered unions, matched geometry transitions, and clever control interactions that elevate your app’s UI. This is hands-on, practical, and comprehensive.

SF Symbols 7 brings powerful new tools to designers and developers working on iOS and macOS 26+. In this hands-on tutorial, I’ll walk you through all the major new features introduced at WWDC25, including the new drawOn and drawOff symbol effects, symbol gradients, Magic Replace transitions, and the brand-new variableValue and symbolVariableMode modifiers.

You’ll learn how to create dynamic and responsive icons with precise control, explore practical examples like an animated countdown timer, and experiment with the new animation capabilities Apple has added for system symbols.

Whether you’re designing for iPhone, iPad, Mac, or even Vision Pro, this update will elevate the polish of your UI. Download the starter project from the link below to follow along, or grab the completed source if you prefer to dive into the code directly.
eVideos.video: What’s New in SF Symbols 7 – Stunning Visual Effects for iOS & macOS 26

eVideos.videoDescription:
Apple’s new Icon Composer, introduced at WWDC25, is a powerful tool for creating layered, liquid-glass icons for iPhone, Mac, Apple Watch, and more—and it’s already bundled inside Xcode 26.

In this video, I’ll walk you through everything you need to know to get started. You’ll learn:
• How to launch Icon Composer (no extra download required)
• How to explore and recreate the Landmarks sample app icon
• How to manage groups, layers, lighting, and preview modes
•How to integrate your custom icons directly into your Xcode projects
• How to use SF Symbols, or PNG assets to design icons

Whether you’re a designer or not, Icon Composer makes it easy to bring your app icons to life with depth, tinting, and platform-specific previews. Plus, I’ll share Apple’s official templates and third-party resources to help streamline your design process.
eVideos.video: Mastering Icon Composer  Create Stunning App Icons

eVideos.videoDescription:
This is the second video in my two-part series on what’s new in Xcode 26. If you haven’t seen the first video—where I covered features available while still on macOS 15—check it out first (link in the description).

In this video, we explore what happens once you upgrade your OS to macOS 26. That’s when the magic begins—enabling Apple Intelligence and unlocking powerful new coding tools like inline explanations, documentation generation, code refactoring, and even generating entire apps from sketches using ChatGPT inside Xcode.

You’ll learn:
• How to enable and connect Apple Intelligence in Xcode 26
• The new Coding Tools sidebar and ChatGPT integration
• Smart code explanations and refactorings
• Context-aware previews and documentation
• Creating a SwiftUI app from a sketch using AI
• The realities and limitations of code assistance

Whether you’re an experienced Swift developer or just curious about what’s possible with Xcode’s AI features, this video offers practical insights and real-world examples.
eVideos.video: What's New in Xcode 26  - Part 2   Intelligence

eVideos.videoDescription:
Explore what’s new in Xcode 26—even if you haven’t yet upgraded to macOS 26.

In this in-depth walkthrough, I’ll show you some of the most significant updates in Xcode 26 that you can use today on macOS 15. We’ll look at the redesigned Start Page, the new iPad-style Settings interface, updated navigation behavior, and a fantastic new tool: the @Playground macro, which lets you test code right inside your project without needing separate playground files.

We’ll also preview how the new Icon Composer integrates with Xcode 26 and demonstrate how to set up modern app icons that respond beautifully to Light, Dark, Tinted, and Clear Home Screen modes—even on iOS 18.5.

And don’t worry—if you’re already on macOS 26, my next video will cover the Intelligence and Code Assist features exclusive to that platform.

Want to take your SwiftUI app to the next level? In this video, I’ll walk you through integrating two of my custom Swift packages: the SF Symbols Picker and the Emoji Picker.

You’ll learn how to install and configure these packages to let your users easily pick from thousands of SF Symbols or a curated set of emojis, all directly within your app. We’ll cover practical use cases like adding emoji-based mood tracking, creating dynamic folder icons with custom colors, and more.

No need to watch the original package series — this video is a complete, standalone guide. Plus, there’s a starter project ready for you to download so you can follow along or jump straight into the completed version.

By the end, you’ll have all the tools you need to provide a seamless and visually engaging selection experience in your apps.
eVideos.video: Supercharge Your SwiftUI App with SF Symbols & Emoji Pickers

eVideos.videoDescription:
Hardcoding API keys into your app? You might want to think twice.
In this tutorial, we’ll build a simple SwiftUI app that uses the Merriam-Webster Thesaurus API to fetch definitions and synonyms for a word. But more importantly, I’ll show you how easily a plaintext API key can be extracted from your compiled app—even without your source code.
To address this, we’ll use SecureVail’s ConfidentialKit to obfuscate your API key with customizable encryption right within your Swift project. I’ll take you through the full setup: installing packages, creating the confidential.yml configuration file, setting up build plugins, and reading your encrypted key safely inside your app.
We’ll also look at how to keep your YAML file out of source control so your keys stay private, even on GitHub.
eVideos.video: How to Obfuscate API Keys in Your Swift Apps Step by Step with ConfidentialKit

eVideos.videoDescription:
Tired of converting between miles and kilometers, Celsius and Fahrenheit, or pounds and kilograms manually? Swift’s Measurement API makes it all effortless — and in this comprehensive tutorial, I’ll show you how to go far beyond the basics.

 We’ll explore:
• How to create and convert measurement values like distance, weight, temperature, and more
 • Performing arithmetic operations safely and accurately using units
 • Formatting output for different locales (🇺🇸🇫🇷🇩🇪)
 • Creating custom units (like football fields!) and entire custom dimensions (like currencies)

Whether you’re building a fitness tracker, a weather app, or a scientific calculator, this video will help you write cleaner, more expressive, and internationalized Swift code.
eVideos.video: Swift’s Measurement API — From Miles to Meters and Beyond

eVideos.videoDescription:
Arrays are great—but they’re not always the right tool for the job. In this video, we dive deep into Sets in Swift, exploring what makes them unique, how to use them effectively, and when to choose them over arrays.

 You’ll learn:
•.How to create and manipulate sets
• The key differences between sets and arrays
• Core operations like insert, remove, union, intersection, and more
• Comparison methods like subset, superset, and disjoint
• Real-world use cases including tag filtering, access permissions, deduplication, and appointment scheduling

By the end, you’ll have a fully working playground and a deeper understanding of when and why to reach for a Set instead of an Array.
eVideos.video: Mastering Swift Sets: A Practical Guide

eVideos.videoDescription:
Renaming an Xcode project after it’s been created can be a real pain. From updating the bundle identifier, target names, entitlements, file structures, and folders—it’s easy to miss something.

In this video, I’ll walk you through a streamlined command line tool that simplifies the entire process. Originally a Swift script by Marco Tatić, I’ve turned it into an installable CLI tool called xprename to make renaming projects faster and more accessible. With just one command, you can rename your entire project, and I’ll show you exactly how it works, step-by-step.

You’ll learn:
	•	Why renaming manually is error-prone
	•	How to use the tool via Terminal
	•	Two easy ways to install: with Homebrew or from source
	•	How the tool works behind the scenes using Swift’s ArgumentParser
eVideos.video: A CommandLine Tool for Renaming Xcode Projects
Customize macOS Folders Like Never Before – Introducing Folder Flare
eVideos.videoDescription:
macOS 26 finally lets us customize folders with icons and colors—but the feature feels a bit… limited. No search for SF Symbols, color tied only to the last-applied tag, and emoji support that’s better—but still not great.

That’s where Folder Flare comes in.

Inspired by a Mastodon post just before WWDC 2025, I decided to build a better solution—with help from ChatGPT. Folder Flare gives you full control over how your folders look, whether you’re running macOS 26 or an earlier version.

✅ Apply SF Symbols with search and color options
✅ Use searchable emojis by category or keyword
✅ Add your own custom images
✅ Rotate, resize, tint, reposition, and more

eVideos.video: Create a Swift Package from Your SwiftUI Project (SF Symbol Picker)
eVideos.videoDescription:
This is the 3rd video in the SFSymbolPicker series.  Do you want to turn your SwiftUI app components into a Swift package you can reuse and share? In this video, I’ll walk you step-by-step through converting a demo project into a Swift package using the SF Symbol Picker as an example.

You’ll learn how to:
 • Structure your project for maintainability
 • Create and configure a multi-platform Swift package
 • Move and expose only what your package needs
 • Handle macOS and iOS differences in SwiftUI
 • Publish your package to GitHub
 • Tag versions and update the README
 • Add your Swift package to another project

This video builds on my previous tutorials, so check the links below for related videos on decoding plists and working with Git and GitHub in Xcode.

eVideos.video: Build a Custom SF Symbol Picker in SwiftUI – Filter by Category & Search!
eVideos.videoDescription:
In the second video of this series, we take our decoded SF Symbols data and use it to build a fully functional SF Symbol Picker in SwiftUI. You’ll learn how to:
* Import and decode plist files from the SF Symbols app
* Build a reusable loader using @Observable
* Create a dynamic picker that filters symbols by category
* Add search functionality to narrow down symbols
* Present your picker using sheets or popovers
* Reuse this picker in any iOS SwiftUI project

This is a practical deep dive into building a SwiftUI component that you’ll actually use — with clean design and flexible configuration.

eVideos.video: 2024-25 Year in Review for StewartLynch Channel
eVideos.videoDescription: As WWDC 2025 kicks off, I’m taking a moment to reflect on everything I’ve created over the past year—over 50 videos, a brand new Swift package, a free multi-platform app, and even my first paid course! Whether you’re new to my channel or a longtime viewer, this quick recap will help you catch up on all the tutorials, deep dives, series, and resources I’ve released since WWDC 2024. Links to everything mentioned are in the description. Thanks for being part of the journey!

eVideos.video: Decode Property Lists in Swift – Essential Prep for Your SF Symbol Picker
eVideos.videoDescription:
We’re starting a brand new series where the end goal is to build a reusable SF Symbol Picker Swift Package that you can drop into any project. In this first video, we’ll lay the groundwork by exploring something crucial in iOS and macOS development—decoding property lists (plists).

You’ll learn how to:
• Create and decode your own plists using PropertyListDecoder
• Understand dictionary vs. array-based plist structures
• Create generic plist decoding functions
• Decode real SF Symbols metadata from Apple’s tools
• Build Swift model structs for symbol categories, search terms, availability, and more

We’ll also take this a step further by consolidating multiple plist sources into a comprehensive Symbol model.

eVideos.video: Elevate Your SwiftUI Lists with iOS 18’s New Container Features
eVideos.videoDescription:
If you’re already familiar with custom container views in SwiftUI, you’re going to love what iOS 18 brings to the table. In this follow-up to my earlier video (linked below), I explore two exciting new additions introduced at WWDC24:
 • Accessing section subviews (headers, content, and footers)
 • Using the new ContainerValue struct for dynamic view behavior

I’ll walk you through two practical examples: enhancing a basic list with stylized sections and creating a dynamic, filterable to-do list using ContainerValue to elevate a selected section to the top.

Along the way, we’ll:
• Build and modularize custom container views
• Use SwiftUI’s new scroll and animation capabilities
• Dynamically group data and style it with conditional logic

Deep Dish Swift 2025 was held on April 27 - 29 in Chicago.  I was fortunate  enough to be one of this year's presenters.
The conference was live streamed and Powered by Tramline.  You can find the entire stream at https://www.youtube.com/@UCFIrollHWTqKEhoHBUTXyaw Plans are in place to create individual videos of each talk but until that time,  conference organizer Josh Holtz has graciously allowed me to extract my talk and post it on my channel.

eVideos.video: Mastering Custom Container Views in SwiftUI – With ViewBuilders, State & Closures
eVideos.videoDescription:
In this Video, you’ll learn how to:
 • Create flexible containers using @ViewBuilder
 • Pass customizable parameters with default values
 • Use view modifiers to replicate container behavior
 • Understand when to use a container view vs. a modifier
 • Inject logic using closures
 • Add internal state to your containers

We’ll build three complete examples:
 1. A styled container with custom colors and SF Symbols
 2. A toggle-based container that holds its own state
 3. A reusable confirmation form container that responds to form state and executes dynamic actions

This is an advanced but practical guide for any SwiftUI developer wanting to create reusable, powerful view components.

eVideos.video: Entry Macro with Binding and Theming for SwiftUI – Fixing Issues
eVideos.videoDescription:
In this video, we improve our SwiftUI theming system by addressing three key issues:
✅ Fixing dark mode inconsistencies
✅ Resolving unwanted background reveals in modal sheets
✅ Persisting the selected theme between app launches

We’ll explore solutions using SwiftUI’s preferredColorScheme, custom presentation detents, and AppStorage with RawRepresentable. By the end of this video, your app’s theming system will be more reliable and user-friendly.

eVideos.video: SwiftUI’s Entry Macro: Simplifying Environment Keys & Theming
eVideos.videoDescription:
In this video, I explore the powerful new @Entry macro introduced in 2024, which simplifies the creation of environment values in SwiftUI while maintaining backward compatibility with iOS 13. I take it a step further by using bindings to introduce a theming system that dynamically updates UI elements across the app.

You’ll learn how to:
✅ Replace boilerplate environment key setup with @Entry
✅ Use bindings in environment values for real-time updates
✅ Implement a theme system with tint and background colors
✅ Programmatically navigate tabs using an environment key

By the end of this video, you’ll have a fully functional theming system and tab navigation using SwiftUI’s modern approach.

eVideos.video: Understanding .contentTransition in SwiftUI – Smoothly Animate Text, Symbols & More!
eVideos.videoDescription:
In this video, I dive into the power of the contentTransition modifier in SwiftUI, introduced in iOS 17. Unlike the transition modifier, contentTransition allows us to animate changes within a view’s content rather than replacing the entire view. This creates smoother and more natural animations for text updates, image changes, and other UI modifications.

We’ll explore five different content transitions:
✅ Numeric Text Transition – Smoothly animate changing numbers like a digital clock.
✅ Symbol Effect Transition – Seamlessly switch between SF Symbols with animations.
✅ Opacity Transition – Fade between different icons, such as a sun and moon.
✅ Interpolate Transition – Animate text color, size, and position smoothly.
✅ Symbol Effect with Options – Enhance symbol transitions with extra effects like bounce.

eVideos.video: Mastering SwiftUI Transitions – Custom & Built-in Animations
eVideos.videoDescription:
In this video, we explore the Transition protocol introduced in iOS 17 and how it allows us to control how views enter and exit the view hierarchy in SwiftUI. We’ll dive into both built-in AnyTransition types and custom transitions, showing how to combine them for more dynamic UI effects.

🔥 What You’ll Learn:
✅ Simple transitions like opacity, slide, move, scale, and offset
✅ Combining transitions for complex effects
✅ Creating custom transitions using the ViewModifier protocol
✅ Using asymmetric transitions for different enter/exit animations
✅ Practical tips for enhancing your SwiftUI apps with smooth UI effects

In this video, I’ll show you how to leverage SwiftUI ViewModifiers to improve code readability, flexibility, and maintainability. We’ll create three custom view modifiers that you can start using in your SwiftUI projects today. Each modifier enhances different aspects of UI development, from embedding views in a navigation stack to styling text editors and applying customizable background views.

By the end of this tutorial, you’ll have a deeper understanding of how ViewModifiers work and how to make your SwiftUI code more reusable and efficient.

eVideos.video: SwiftUI Overtop Picker with Protocols – A Flexible Alternative to Modal Sheets
eVideos.videoDescription:
In this video, I take my original Overtop Picker View solution and improve upon it using Swift protocols. I’ll show you how to create a flexible view modifier that allows you to present a custom edit view using a picker, a date picker, or even a struct for editing. This approach is a great alternative to traditional modal sheet views, making your SwiftUI apps more dynamic and reusable!

📌 Topics Covered:
	•	Using protocols to define reusable Overtoppable views
	•	Creating generic view modifiers for multiple edit types
	•	Building Overtop Color Picker, Profile Editor, and Date Picker views
	•	Improving code organization and reusability with code snippets
	•	Handling optional values in SwiftUI

eVideos.video: Creating an Over Top View in SwiftUI: A Unique Way to Present Edit Views
eVideos.videoDescription:
Sometimes your UI calls for a bit of creativity! Instead of using a modal sheet or a navigation stack, you can display an Over Top View—an overlay that allows you to edit content while still seeing the original view behind it.

In this video, I’ll show you how to implement an Over Top View in SwiftUI, which prevents interaction with the background while providing a clean and intuitive way to make updates. We’ll cover:
✅ Structuring the Over Top View
✅ Creating a reusable view modifier
✅ Using state properties for smooth transitions
✅ Handling updates efficiently with closures

This is Part 1 of a two-part series. In the next video, we’ll enhance this solution to make it generic and more versatile so it can handle more than just string-based pickers!

eVideos.video: A case for Custom Bindings in SwiftUI: Essential Tips and Tricks
eVideos.videoDescription:
In this video, I’ll show you why Custom Bindings in SwiftUI are a powerful tool you should master! While they may seem intimidating at first, I’ll break them down into easy-to-understand examples that will help you integrate them seamlessly into your SwiftUI projects.

We’ll cover:
✅ Creating custom bindings for optional values (String, Int, Date)
✅ Binding computed properties for better control
✅ Using bindings in ViewModels for better state management
✅ Improving efficiency and clarity with inline binding syntax

By the end of this tutorial, you’ll have a solid reference project that you can keep coming back to whenever you need to implement custom bindings.

eVideos.video: Create Custom Tab Bars in SwiftUI – An Alternative to Default Tabs!
eVideos.videoDescription:
Tired of the standard SwiftUI TabView? In this video, I’ll show you how to replace the default tab bar with custom-designed tab bars that work on iOS and iPadOS! 
What You’ll Learn:

✅ How to hide the default Tab Bar
✅ Creating custom tab bars with animations
✅ Using SwiftUI enums & bindings for cleaner navigation
✅ Solving issues like the More button & extra tabs
✅ Designing three custom tab bar styles

eVideos.video: Enum-Driven Tab Views in SwiftUI: A Smarter Approach
eVideos.videoDescription:
Want to build a cleaner, more maintainable tab view in SwiftUI? In this video, I’ll show you how to use enums that conform to the View protocol to power your TabView more efficiently! 🚀
What You’ll Learn:

✅ How to structure your TabView using enums
✅ Making your enums Identifiable & CaseIterable
✅ Binding selection state for dynamic tab navigation
✅ Implementing environment objects for seamless tab switching

eVideos.video: How to Create a Custom GPT with Your Own Knowledge Base
eVideos.videoDescription:
In this video, I’ll show you how to create your own Custom GPT using ChatGPT Pro, and how you can upload your own knowledge base to make it even more powerful! I’ll walk you through the process of setting up your GPT, adding content (like video transcripts), and even automating transcript downloads using Python scripts.

📌 What You’ll Learn:
✅ How to create a Custom GPT with OpenAI
✅ Uploading text, PDFs, Markdown, and CSV files
✅ Using Python scripts to fetch YouTube transcripts
✅ Setting up a Google API Key for video data
✅ Consolidating transcript files for easy upload

eVideos.video: Mastering Image Views in SwiftUI – Assets, Bundles, Remote URLs & Effects
eVideos.videoDescription:
In this SwiftUI tutorial, we dive deep into everything you need to know about working with images in SwiftUI. From loading images from your asset catalog and app bundle to fetching remote images from a URL, we cover it all! Plus, we’ll explore image effects, template images, and how to apply modifiers like resizing, clipping, masking, and blending.

🔹 Topics Covered:
✅ Loading images from Assets
✅ Fetching images from the Bundle
✅ Loading images from the Documents directory
✅ Displaying remote images with AsyncImage
✅ Clipping and masking images
✅ Using template images with dynamic tint colors
✅ Applying special effects like blur, saturation, and blend modes

eVideos.video: Enhancing the Custom Help System in SwiftUI Without Breaking Existing Projects
eVideos.videoDescription:
In this video, I enhance the custom help system I created in a previous tutorial, ensuring it remains backward-compatible with existing projects. The improvements include customizable button colors and symbols, adjustable image sizes using containerRelativeFrame, and support for multiple help options using menus.
🛠 Topics Covered:
✔️ Customizing the Help Button’s appearance (color & symbol)
✔️ Using enum for predefined symbol selections
✔️ Implementing containerRelativeFrame for adaptive image sizing
✔️ Supporting multiple help options via Menu
✔️ Using variadic parameters for a flexible API

eVideos.video: How to Create a Custom Help System in SwiftUI – A Reusable Solution for Your Apps
eVideos.videoDescription:
In this video, I’ll show you how to build a custom help system in SwiftUI that can be incorporated into any of your projects. You’ll learn how to create a floating help button, use an enum-based approach for help content, and design a help view with a smooth paging system.

By the end of this video, you’ll have a fully reusable help system that requires only two lines of code to implement in any SwiftUI view! 🚀

📌 What You’ll Learn:
	•	How to create a help page struct for text and images
	•	Using an enum to manage different help cases
	•	Implementing a floating help button with a view modifier
	•	Designing a help screen with Markdown support
	•	Building custom page indicators for navigation

eVideos.video: self vs. Self in Swift – Everything You Need to Know!
eVideos.videoDescription:
Are you confused about when to use self (lowercase) versus Self (uppercase) in Swift? You’re not alone! In this video, we’ll break down the key differences and teach you when and why to use each one. Whether you’re handling instance properties, working with closures, or dealing with protocols and return types, understanding self and Self will make your Swift code cleaner and more efficient.

What You’ll Learn:
✅ When and why to use self in Swift
✅ How self helps with closures and escaping functions
✅ The role of Self in protocols, factory methods, and extensions
✅ Practical real-world examples to make everything clear

In SwiftUI, a Color is a view used to display a rectangular area of a specific color. It is not just a data structure for color values like UIColor in UIKit; instead, it is an actual view component that conforms to the View protocol. This makes it more than just a way to define colors—it is a lightweight and flexible way to fill parts of your SwiftUI interface with color.

Whether you’re designing a simple app or a complex user interface, colors play a huge role in enhancing the look and feel of your design. They can guide users, set the mood, and make your app stand out. But did you know that SwiftUI gives us multiple ways to define and use colors? From built-in static colors like .primary and .secondary, to creating custom colors using RGB, HSB, and even Hex values, the possibilities are endless.

I'm also going to cover how to access UIKit colors that aren’t directly available in SwiftUI—yes, you can still use your favorite UIColor.systemTeal in a SwiftUI project! And to top it off, I’ll show you how to adapt colors dynamically for light and dark modes, making your app look amazing no matter what theme the user has set.

Specifically, I want to show you how you consider replacing the majority of print statements you may have in your projects with OSLog

Learn how to download and maintain multiple versions of Xcode and learn about the new features available in Xcode 15 so you can start taking advantage of new workflows and features introduced for iOS and iPadOS 17, WatchOS 10 and macOS 14

Over the past 15 weeks, I have been focussing on producing swift and swiftUI content on topics that I had a working knowledge of but I always had the feeling that there was something that I was missing, or not completely understanding so I thought that I would finish this series off by presenting a quick overview of each video and provide links to all of them.

In this video I want to introduce you to and explain what an inout parameter is in Swift.
In the process, we will look at some practical use cases and also explore cases where using inout is not allowed and, how functions with inout  parameters transition to mutating functions in a struct.

In this video, I want to show you how you can use AlignmentGuides in SwiftUI to align views differently in your UI.
We will start with the basics and of AlignmentGuides on the VStack, HStack and ZStack containers.
Next we will discover how you can adjust subviews of the container stack and transform the alignment in the direction of the container's alignment either towards or away from it.
We will follow that by looking at how we can adjust the subviews positions even further using an alignmentGuides ViewDimensions struct that provides us with both  the dimensions of the view, but also access to the actual alignment guide's through the subscript of the viewDimension.
We will finish off by showing you how you can create your own custom AlignmentGuides so you can align views in one container with views or alignment guides of other container views.

In this video I am going to explore two related view modifier methods.  The first being the ignoreSafeArea method and the second being the safeAreaInset modifier.  Both return new views for the ones they are applied to.  Just like other view modifiers.
And, as usual. There might be one or more tidbits in this video to show you something else you may not be aware of, but might be useful in your projects.

In this video, I want to look at Variadic parameters in Swift.
If you are not clear of exactly what variadic parameters are, and how to use them, then this might help you.
Also, if you think you have never used variadic parameters in your code, then you are mistaken because I am pretty sure you have and as a bonus, we will take that knowledge and extend it to be something even more useful so stick with me until the end.

In this video, I want to introduce you to swift subscripts
 I will step you through the basics as they apply to arrays and dictionaries so that you get a general understanding off what subscripts are and how they are used with Swift collections.
I will then show you how you can create your own custom subscripts and in the process share how you can use subscripts to make your code safer and more generic.
We will finish this by creating two rather useful extensions.  One for String and one for Arrays and both are extensions using subscripts.

In this video I will introduce you to NameSpaces and the SwiftUI matchedGeometryEffect method where you can create stunning transitions from one  view to another and make your apps sparkle and fun to use.
Learn all about how the matchedGeometryEffect properties work and follow examples on how you can implement it in your own projects.

eVideos.video: The Year In Review and Looking Ahead
eVideos.videoDescription: An overview of the past year since WWDC 22 and the content that I provided.

In this video, I want to try and clarify what a GeometryReader is in SwiftUI and how you might use it.
I will compare geometryReaders to other ContainerViews so that you will see that it has two big difference.
It is aware of it's own coordinate space, namely it's position and size, but also all views within the container are laid out differently from other container views.
By the end of this video you should have a better understanding of what a GeometryReader is and be less intimidated as I was before I researched this video.

In this tutorial, I am going to introduce you to SwiftUI PreferenceKeys. If you've been creating SwiftUI applications for a while, you might have been using them without even realizing it.
Firstly, I will explain what a preferenceKey is and demonstrate how you have been utilizing them in your own projects since the early stages of SwiftUI development. It's fascinating to discover the hidden power behind these essential tools.
Next, I will delve into the structure and requirements for creating custom PreferenceKeys. I'll guide you through the process and show you how to utilize the Reduce function to send information up your view hierarchy instead of the traditional approach of passing down variables through the environment.
To make things more practical and engaging, I will provide four examples throughout the video. Some of these examples may seem contrived, but they serve the purpose of showcasing the true potential of preference keys. You'll gain a solid understanding of their capabilities and how they can be effectively integrated into your own applications.
By the end of this tutorial, you'll have a clear grasp of SwiftUI PreferenceKeys and the immense value they bring to your development workflow.

eVideos.video: Formatting Date Strings in Swift and SwIftUI
eVideos.videoDescription:
In this video we are going to explore Swift Dates and how you can format dates as strings for presentation in your Swift / SwiftUI projects.
We will look at the  DateFormatter class and it's dateStyle and timeStyle properties.
This will be followed by using fixed format date representations using a format string.
In iOS 14 with SwiftUI we got an easier way to display dates In text views so we will explore the formatter initializer that was introduced.
In iOS 15 this expanded even more so that we can now use the static dateTime of the Date.formatStyle structure and the format initializer for a Text view.

In this video we are going to explore how we can stylize text for our Text views in SwiftUI.
We will start by looking at how we can create a `Text` view with the Markdown-formatted base language version of the string as the localization key,
We will also see how we can utilize string interpolation to combine and stylize our strings and present them in a text view.
And finally, we will take a quick look at the power of Attributed strings in SwiftUI.

eVideos.video: Type Extensions in Swift and SwiftUI
eVideos.videoDescription:
In this video we are going to explore Type Extensions for Swift and SwiftUI.
We will look at the three different types of extensions for types that  allow you to extend the capabilities of a type by adding new methods, properties or subscripts.

In this video, I want to introduce you to KeyPaths and how you can use them in your Swift projects.
We will start by looking a what a KeyPath is and how you can use them to reference to a property of an object or a struct and then look at some examples of how you might apply them in your code.
This will include using keyPaths for sorting and mapping arrays, we will look at  the DynamicMemberLookup attribute and  two very practical examples for using KeyPaths to simplify your code
We will finish with a short explanation of how keyPaths are used in Lists for SwiftUI

As part of the Swift Deeper Understanding series I want to take a closer look at Initializers
We will take a look at what an initializer is for structs and classes and we will look at creating multiple initializers for a struct or class and find out what a Convenience initializer is.
We will finish the video by looking at how we can create a custom initializer for a SwiftUI HStack

In this video I want to show you how you can locate and update files that are stored in the Data Folder of the simulator, but also the preview provider, and, as a bonus, I will show you how you can move files stored in the documents directory and the Application Support directory for applications you have created and have running on your ipHone (like Core Data SQLLite files) to your Xcode Simulator locations.

In this video I want to help you understand trailing closures and swift's trailing closure syntax and to help you make sense of some of the different initializers for controls like buttons and lists in SwiftUI.
You often hear people talk about making your code more Swifty.  What exactly does that mean?  I suppose it means different things to different people, but really, what it means is to write idiomatic Swift and by this, I mean to write code that looks and feels like Swift including swift specific language constructs and conventions and to avoid void patterns that might be more ore common in other programming languages.
A big part of this is the trailing closure syntax that is used.
As swift evolves, the language changes.  As recent as Swift 5.3, the introduction to multiple trailing closures made for a simpler way to call a function with several closures and this made for simpler, more readable constructors for things like buttons.

In this video I hope to share with you some things that you may not know or have forgotten about SwiftUI previews and what changed in Xcode 14 so that you can get the most out of creating and viewing your SwiftUI Views while designing and coding them.
If you want to support my work, you can buy me a coffee :)
https://ko-fi.com/stewartlynch
In this video I want show you what tuples are in Swift and provide you with some practical examples that you may consider using in your existing or future projects.

eVideos.video: 1. SwiftUI Coding Workshop 1: Introduction and Xcode Overview
eVideos.videoDescription:
This workshop and series of exercises to build 3 SwiftUI iOS applications will help you improve your development skills and introduce you to some best practices.
This workshop is not intended for absolute beginners, but the content is arranged in such a way that if your experience is limited, you will be able to cut and paste code from the provided documentation without getting left behind.
You will have access to the all of the completed applications and documentation for your own personal or instructional use after the workshop is completed.
In addition, the documentation provides links to several supplementary videos on several of the topics covered.

eVideos.video: My Images CD Part 7 - CloudKit Sync with Core Data
eVideos.videoDescription:
In this video we will be configuring our persistent container so that it will synchronize our Core Data entity to CloudKit.
This means that you will be able to run the app on all of your devices that are signed in to your iCloud account and be able to create, view, update and delete your my Image objects including the images have have those updates synched across all of the devices.

eVideos.video: My Images CD (Storing images in Core Data) Part 6
eVideos.videoDescription:
In the first 5 vidoes of this series, we saved our images to the application's documents directory.  I have had many request to update this to show how you can store your images as data right within Core Data, so that is what we are going to do in this video.
We will add a new image attribute to our CoreData model and create a Value Transformer so we can easily  transform our data into a UIImage when reading and back to data when adding or updating images.

In this video I am going to show you how you can create your own custom Environment Values
We will learn the basics and then create our own environment value that will allow us to apply a different theme to our app based on a particular in app purchase.

In this video I will introduce you to Lottie 4.0, Lottie  is Airbnb’s cross-platform, open-source  library for rendering vector motion graphics.  Lottie is used extensively at Airbnb, and it also powers animations in thousands of other apps throughout the industry. 
In this video, I will take you through my learning process for building a UIViewRepresentable so you can easily implement Lottie animations into your SwiftUI apps.

eVideos.video: Persisting to JSON or MarkDown in SwiftUI
eVideos.videoDescription: In this video I am going to be showing you how you can choose to persist your application data to your documents directory in the typical JSON format and also as MarkDown using a SwiftPackage called MarkCodable.  As you will see there are some real advantages to being able to view and edit your saved data as markdown.

eVideos.video: My Images Core Data (Sharing Images) Part 5
eVideos.videoDescription: This is the final video in this part of the My Images with Core Data series.  In this video we will see how we can email one of your myImage objects including both the json and image payload to another user and see how upon receipt, the user can quickly have it added to their own application Core Data store and the image to the app's document directory

eVideos.video: My Images Core Data (Sharing Images) Part 4
eVideos.videoDescription:
This is the 4th video but the 2nd one in this current section of the my Images with core data series
In this video we will be seeing how we can respond to opening documents that have been received from other devices or application for types that our app will recognize.
We will decode the JSON received and create a new object in our version of the app, then we will take the next step to see how we can zip up both the json and the image before sending and then reverse the process on receipt.

eVideos.video: My Images Core Data (Sharing Images) Part 3
eVideos.videoDescription:
This is a continuation of the My Images Core Data series.
In this 3 part continuation of this series, we will be adding the ability to share your favourite images with other users of your app by creating a unique file that you can share as an email attachment  to anyone else who has your app.  When they receive the email and tap in the attachment, the user will be given the option of opening it using the app and have the image and all information about the image added to their Core Data database and the image to their documents directory
In this first video we will be adding new attributes to our Core Data entity and create a Universal Type Identifier that will be able to identify the content of your application's file that we will create for sharing.
We will see how the receiving device will recoginze files of that type and automatically open when receiving the new content.

In this video I am going to show you how I handle textfields for iOS and iPADOS in SwiftUI when I want to restrict entry to either integer or decimal values only.
There are some real issues with using TextFields in SwiftUI when you want to limit the entry to either an integer or a decimal value.  As we work through this project I will show you what those issues are and how I overcome them with a  Toolbar button, a view Modifier and UIKit trick.

Learn how you can capitalize the power of enums and the new NavigationStack in iOS 16 to streamline and manage your navigation.
Learn about Enum conformance to the String, Hashable, CaseIterable, and Identifiable and View protocols.

My iOS 16 Playlist has over 7.5 hours of content on new iOS 16 features.  In this summary video, I give you a very brief overview of what you can expect to learn by viewing and working along with the video.  Links to all videos are below.

In this video we are going to be looking at how we can use the new requestReview environment value to get an instance of the RequestReviewAction struct so that we can have the app make that request on our behalf. 
I will also show you how you can provide your users with a button that you can provide your users so that they can submit a review at any time.
Along the way, we will discover some new iOS 16 features as well such as presentation detents, navigation Toolbar modifiers and and a new Task sleep function.

In this video I am going to be showing you the new AnyLayout; the type-erased instance of the layout protocol that allows you to dynamically change the type of layout container without destroying the stat of the subviews.
In addition to the standard HStack, VStack and ZStack layout types we will also be creating our own Custom Layout to add to the mix.

This is the second of two videos where I show you how you can save images to your documents directory and keep a record of that in a CoreData Database.
In this video, we will be completing the project by creating the final component for our form presentation method by using an enum to determine if we are updating our creating new objects.
We will add actions for all CRUD operations and complete the design of our presentation grid view.

This is a first of a two part series to demonstrate an option for  how you deal with Images when your persistence layer is something like CoreData or Realm?
Images can be large and putting all of your eggs in one basket so to speak is not a great idea both from a performance point of view and, your database becomes really large very quickly.

The prevailing recommendation is to store your images locally to your documents directory and just keep a reference to that image stored as a property of one of your database records.
This works well for both Realm and CoreData, two offline persistence data sources that I use.
In this tutorial, I am going to be using CoreData as it requires no third party packages.

In this video, we will be finding out how we can use the Live Text feature to scan and copy text from images on our phones or iPad cameras.
We will use VisionKit to present the camera and allow us to capture any text it finds.  This will be implemented  by creating a DataScanViewController using A UIViewControllerRepresentable.
Similarly in the In the second part of the video we will again use VisionKit to scan an image, looking for text using a  UIViewRepresentable to create a UIImageView that will allow us to analyze the image selected from our Photos album.

In this video I am going to introduce you to the new Gauge view that is now available for all apple platforms in iOS 16
We will be exploring the different options for Linear gauges as well as circular gauges and will compete the video by creating a fun view with a countdown timer to launch a rocket.

In this video, I am going to introduce you to  ShareLink which was introduced in iOS 16 and it is a much simpler way to gather information from your app that you may which to share with others via the ShareSheet option.
We will look at the basic initializers and what affect each of the arguments have when sharing via a text message or email and then we will take a look at a more practical example.

In this video we dive into the iOS ImageRenderer frameworks for SwiftUI.
Learn how to generate images from your views and share them using the new ShareLink method introduced in iOS 16
We will be looking at generating images from our views and I will be using 2 different examples
One will be to generate an image from a view that has a fixed frame size and the other where the view's size is determined by the amount of space made available by the device screen and layout.
We will look at some best practices for avoiding issues with transparency and resolution.

In this video I am going to be showing you the new ViewThatFits container view in SwiftUI/
ViewThatFits automatically measures available space and the size of its children and takes the first view that perfectly fits the available space. That’s it.  Very simple
What I want to do today is to go over some practical examples to show you what this means and how you might want to use it in your own.

If you are looking to add tables to your SwiftUI projects then this is the video for you.  Learn how to implement tables for iPad in iOS 16 but also how to deal with those apps that also support iPhones.   We will be covering all of the basics and reveal work arounds to issues I discovered.  Learn also how to embed tables in a NavigationStack and a NavigationSplitView.

This is the final video in the 3 part iOS Navigation series for iOS 16.  In the first two videos we focussed on the NavigationStack but in this video, we will be looking at NavigationSplitView.
We will see how we can implement 2 column and 3 column split view that  will compress down to a NavigationStack type navigation when the view width is compressed like on all iPhones in Portrait mode or on some split views on an iPad.
We will see how we can control the visibility of the different views and layouts.

This is the second video in the 3 part ioS 16 Navigation Series.  In the first video we learned about the NavigationStack and all of it's components and in this video we will be extending that knowledge
We will extending the Navigation stack another level and see how we can use the NavigationPath to implement a Back to Root button.
Following that, we will see how easy it is to use the NavigationPath to enable programmable navigation through Deep links using a Custom URL Scheme

This is the first of 3 videos in a new iOS 16 series on the new Navigation api in iOS 16
In this video I will introduce yu to the Navigation Stack
We will take a look at this new container view along with its components.  Namely the new NavigationLink. the navigationdestination method and the navigationPath
In the 2nd video of this series we will stay with the navigationStack and look more into programmable navigation and using deep links from external sources to open and navigation to view in your apps.
In the 3rd and final video in this series, we will look at the new NavigationSplitView container that will allow us to present 2 and 3 column navigation views on larger devices while still falling back to a traditional NavigationStack on narrower ones.

In this video I am going to introduce you to the Grid View for SwiftUI that was introduced in iOS 16.
We will take a look at three different examples, exploring all of the grid building blocks.
We will learn about: 
* The Grid container itself
* The Grid Row
* Grid  layouts using grid alignments
* Cell positioning with cell alignments and anchors.
* Full column alignments
* Merging cells using column spans

In this video, I am going to introduce you to the new bottom sheet presentationDetents modifier that was introduced in iOS 16.  This will gives us the ability to control the height of our modal sheets.
I will introduce you to detents and all of their options and  create a custom view modifier to optionally add a close button to any one of your sheets.
We will look at different sheet view presentation overloads and finally, how you can create your own custom detent.

In this video, I am going to introduce you to the new PhotosPicker for SwiftUI that was introduced in iOS 16.
The PhotosPicker struct is a view that displays a Photos picker for choosing assets from the photo library.
In iOS 15. we had PHPicker for UIKit and to use that in SwiftUI, we had to wrap it in a UIViewRepresentable, but with iOS 16, we can now do that in SwiftUI.
In this video, I will introduced you to a variety of image formats and show you how you can implement a SwiftUI photo picker for single or multiple images at a time.

This is the second video in my introduction to the SwiftUI Charts framework introduced in iOS 16
In this video, I will take a look at how we can better present large data sets to your users by way of bar charts.
Along the way, I will introduce you to many customizations that you can add to your charts.
This is a particularly long video and there is no need to watch it all the way through.  I have chapter links in the video so take your time.
eVideos.video: Video 2: Charts Framework 2 - Visualizing Large Data Sets with Bar Charts

eVideos.videoDescription:
This is the first of a two part series where I explore the new Charts framework introduced in iOS 16 and specifically, the BarChart type of chart.
In this first video, I will focus solely on the Charts framework how Bar Charts are created in order to build a concrete basis and understanding that you will be able to put to use in your own projects.
In the second video we will do just that.  I am currently redesigning one of my own apps, My Wine Cellar and want to replace a UIKit chart framework with the new SwiftUI version.  I will provide you with the data and we will exlpore different ways of grouping and presenting that data in Bar Charts.

In this video I am going to be covering two distinct by related things.  How to present a Grouped List view and how to add mock data to your previews in SwiftUI
We will start by creating a simple model and some sample object to display in a list
We will then visit the Mocaroo mock data generator site to generate a lot more data to add to our projec
With a lot of data we can then start to display our list differently by grouping and displaying it in collapsible groups.

And all the while make sure that the data within the groups are all sorted as we like within that section group.
eVideos.video: Grouped Lists and Mock Data in SwiftUI

eVideos.videoDescription:
This is the third video in the Adapty in app subscription purchase series for SwiftUI.  Links to the other two videos are in the description below.
In this video I will introduce you to the powerful paywall remote config feature where you can set values in your paywall that can dynamically change the appearance of your paywall without having to submit a new version of your app to the App Store.
We will also look at creating a second paywall with reduced products to offer your users in a particular scenario.

eVideos.videoDescription:
This is the 2nd in this series on how you can add in-app subscriptions to your SwiftUI app using Adapty, a 3rd party SDK for StoreKit purchases and a good alternative to RevenueCat..
In this video we will design and create a paywall so our users can purchase a subscription.
We will be testing on a real device so you will have to make sure that you have a developer account and set up a Sandbox user.
If you want to follow along, I highly recommend that you watch the first video and complete the starter project so you can test on your own devices.
eVideos.video: 2. In-App Purchases with Adapty 2 - Building the Paywall and making a purchase

eVideos.videoDescription:
Adapty - №1 alternative to RevenueCat. https://adapty.io/ 
Let’s learn how to implement in-app purchases and subscriptions in your iOS app.
Adapty is extremely easy to use, we’ll cover the entire process in this series of videos.
* In part 1, this video I will show you how to configure App Store Connect to enable subscriptions for your application.
* I will show you how you can then configure Adapty to connect to the App Store and manage the purchase on your behalf
* Then, before we move on to designing our interface on our app, I will test to make sure that we have completed the configuration property
In the second video I will show you how you can monetize your app with a subscription in-app purchase and design and  implement a paywall within our app to provide your users the opportunity to take advantage of that.
We will test on a real device using a Sandboxed user that we create in App Store Connect.
In the 3rd video, I will show you how you can add multiple paywalls and using a remote configuration in Adapty to update your paywall's appearance without having to to submit a new version of your app
eVideos.video: 1. In-App Purchases with Adapty 1- Setup App Store Connect and Adapty

eVideos.videoDescription:
In this video, I am going to show you how you can add the new UICalendarView introduced in  iOS 16 for UIKit into a SwiftUI project.  
We are going to convert a simple List View of events that have a date property along with a string and event type to a calendarView displaying decorations around the dates where events occur
I will show you how you can ensure that when you add, update and delete events, their position and decoration on the calendar will update as  well.

This is the fourth video in the Local Notification series.  In this video we will see how we can provide data from the app to the notification and be able to allow the users to choose actions in response the information provided or postpone the notification until  al later time.
We will be diving into the userInfo dictionary that can be added to  notification request content
We can use this to direct users to different views in your app.
We will also be looking at actions that will provide the user with a couple of options to delay the notification reminder until some time later.
eVideos.video: 4. Swift Local Notifications 4: Responding to Notifications

eVideos.videoDescription:
This is the third video in the Local Notifications series for Swift. and SwiftUI
In this video we will be investigating Calendar Notifications.
We are going to refactor our LocalNotification object to handle both the interval and calendar types of triggers and we will create two initializers to do this
We will take a look a dateComponents and how they affect the schedule and make the corresponding changes to the scheduling function in our notification manager class.

We are going to be extending our Dad Jokes application even further.  Currently we have a MacOS target for the Menu Bar version and an iOS Target for the iPhone/iPad version
In this video, we are going to be adding another new target to our app. We are going to create a Widget using WidgetKit.
This widget will use a WidgetIntent to allow users to choose which type of joke they want displayed on the widget and we will use the widgetTimeLine to refresh the joke every 30 minutes or so.
eVideos.video: Building the WidgetKit Target - The Dad Jokes Series (Part 3)

eVideos.videoDescription:
This is the second in a series of videos on scheduling an responding to local notifications in swift
In this video our focus will be on Interval notifications.
We will start by forming a LocalNotification request and then in order to execute the notification, we will need to form a trigger based on that time interval.
Once we have those components in place, we need to schedule it by adding it to the notification queue.
We will also make sure that we see our notifications when the app is in the foreground as well as the when in the background
We will also look at how we can get a list of pending requests and how we cam delete one or more of them.
eVideos.video: 2. Swift Local Notifications 2: Time Interval Notifications

eVideos.videoDescription:
This is the first video in a series that will cover the creation and presentation of local notifications in SwiftUI
In this series, we will be covering a number of topics so that by the end, you will have created a Notification Manager class that you can add to any one of your project to help implement Local Notifications.
We will start with the very important Authorization process and how you can watch for and manage changes to that state for yoru apps.
In the second video, we will cover simple intervcal based notifications
The third will go over calendar based notifications based on date components, and the fourth video will show you how you can pass app payload data to the notification and create actions that will allow you to respond to tap events on the notification.

eVideos.video: Guard vs If Explained in Swift
eVideos.videoDescription:
In this video, I am going to show you the difference between using an if condition and a guard condition.
We will look at the pros and cons of each while looking at execution flow, unwrapping optionals and dealing with throwing errors.

eVideos.videoDescription: In this video I am going to show you how you can use  GitHub  to post a blog or product documentation directly to the Web with the Pages option.  I will be demonstrating this by using Typora to convert a markdown file to html and pushing it up to the GitHub repository.

In this video, we are going to take a look at a few things, but the primary goal is to develop a method for presenting a form view that will allow us to either create a new object or update an existing object of the same type.
We will be looking at creating a form along with a FormViewModel that will help us do that along with an enum that conforms to the SwiftUI view protocol so we can use it to present the form for the correct purpose, either an update or a new object
In addition, we will also be seeing how we can use keyPaths for properties in our ViewModel so that we can control the field focus in our form.

eVideos.video: Promote your SwiftUI Apps with SKOverlay
eVideos.videoDescription:
In this video I am going to introduce you to  SKOverlay for SwiftUI, Apple's Swift Class that allows you to recommend another app via an overlay view on top of the current view.
We will start with the basics and review your options and then create a reusable class that you can use in all of your projects that will only display the overlay at a specified interval instead of every time the view appears.

In this video I am going to introduce you to Disclosure Groups in SwiftUI.
I will start with a basic example and show how you can stylize them, and also show you you can programatically control the expansion and collapse of a group.
We will complete the video with a practical example where we convert a boring list view of items to a grouped list using disclosure groups that will allow for collapsing an expansion of data.

SwiftLint is an open-source tool to enforce Swift style and conventions. It is developed by Realm. You can set your coding style rules and force them during development. 
It is based on the now no longer active GitHub Swift StyleGuide that was an attempt to encourage patterns that accomplish the following goals (in rough priority order):
1. Increased rigor, and decreased likelihood of programmer error
2. Increased clarity of intent
3. Reduced verbosity
4. Fewer debates about aesthetics
In this tutorial, I will step you through the process of installing SwiftLint on your mac and how you can start using it to clean up your code.

eVideos.video: In-App Subscriptions in SwiftUI made easy with Glassfy - Part 2 - Creating the Paywall
eVideos.videoDescription:
This the second video in the in 2 part in-app purchase series using Glassfy with SwiftUI.
In this video,  we will build a paywall for our app so your users can make that purchase to unlock the full features of your app.
We will test the purchase and restore of a past purchase using a Sandboxed user on a real device

eVideos.video: In-App Subscriptions in SwiftUI made easy with Glassfy - Part 1 - Setup
eVideos.videoDescription:
This is the first video in a two part series where we look at adding in-app purchase subscriptions to a SwiftUI app using Glassfy.  In this video we will focus on the AppStore Connect app setup and the glassfy setup so that your app can communicate with the AppStore though glassfy's simple process.
By the end of these videos, you will understand why I will never use the native storekit SDK directly in my apps again because there is a simpler, better solution.
In the second video, we will build a paywall for our app so your users can make that purchase to unlock the full features of your app.

SwiftUI's canvas is great as you get to see the changes in the UI when you make them in your code.
This is not always optimal however, and sometimes those previews fail and you have to launch your app to run in the simulator to see what is going on.
Wouldn't it be great if Xcode supported Hot Reloading in the simulator so that you could make changes to the code of your running application and see those changes reflected in the simulator?
Hot reloading is about getting rid of compiling your whole application and avoiding deploy/restart cycles as much as possible while allowing you to edit your running application code and see changes reflected immediately.

This, the 5 video in the Realm with SwiftUI series, I will be introducing you to some more core topics.  We will take a look at how we can utilize the realm configuration to specify a different name for our default realm and we will be replacing an ObservedResults property wrapper with a Notification Token and use a class adhering to the ObservableObject protocol to observe and manage changes.
We will also be utilizing realm's isInvalidated property to ensure smooth operation of our application.

This is the 3rd and final video in a series where we look at ways in which we can get a handle on the complexities of Xcode. In this video we will focus on the code editor
We will look at ways to move around your code and organize it so that you can do a better job of maintaining it in the future.
Throughout this video, I will introduce you to some new keyboard shortcuts but I will also be using ones that I covered in previous videos so make sure you watch those ones too.

This is the second video in the two part project where we are building a simple application in SwiftUI that uses Realm for our data store and focuses on implementing a one-to-many relationship.
If you have not yet watched the first video, I recommend that you do that first.  This video extends from that video and uses the completed project so far.  I have also provided a link to that completed project if you wish to download and start from there in this video.
We have a few things to accomplish in this video. 
*  enable rearranging cities in the cities listview
*  allow for deleting of countries
* inverse relationships
*  adding new properties to a realm database and perform a migration when the app launches.

This is my 3rd video in how to use MongoDb Realm in your SwiftUI projects.
Realm is a NoSQL database much like Firebase Firestore.  It is not the traditional Relational Database model like MySQL and PostreSQL are.
However, that does not mean that you can't create one to many or many to many type relationships with Realm.
In this video we will be introducing a new **List** element type that allows you to create a 1 to many relationship from one model to another.
We will also introduce inverse relationships to provide back links from the many back to the one using **LinkingObjects**

eVideos.video: Building a macOS Menu Bar App - The Dad Jokes Series (Part 1)
eVideos.videoDescription: In this video you will learn how to create and distribute your own menu bar apps for macOS.  This is an app that runs from and is attached to an icon in the Mac’s menu bar.  You likely have many of these in your menu. We will be building an app that fetches random dad jokes and presents them to you in a view attached to your menu.  Learn how to add custom menus with SwiftUI and take advantage of the built-in About and Quit menu types.  In addition you will learn how to notarize your app so you can share it with your friends without having to go through the app store.

eVideos.video: Taming Xcode -2:  Keyboard Shortcuts, File Management and Focus
eVideos.videoDescription:
This is the 2nd of 3 videos in a series where we look at ways in which we can get a handle on the complexities of Xcode. In this video we will focus on Essential keyboard commands and file management.
The objective is to keep our hands on the keyboards so we can focus on our work and make sure that we organize our file structure so that we can quickly locate and manage our code

This is the second video in the Realm with SwiftUI series.  This is actually the second part of using ObserveResults to build a ToDo app.
In this video, you will be introduced to Realm Studio so you can see your realm data in a GUI interface
We will also complete our application by introducing the @ObservedRealmObject property Wrapper along with completing our CRUD operations for updating and deleting objects from our todo list
In addition you will learn about SortDescripters for sorting your results and be introduced to a searchable function for filtering the results in the list.
This is a continuation from the first video in this series so if you have not completed that video, I suggest ou do.  A link is in the description below.  I have also provided a link to the completed project from the first video if you want to use it.
